clue.text: Arrogant at university? Nonsense!

parts.note: being up means in residence at university, in old British usage
pish is an old exclamation dismissing something as nonsense

explanation.surface: A student is accused of arrogance and replies with a scornful dismissal.
explanation.definitionFit: Uppish describes someone haughty or self-assertive, a synonym for arrogant.

clue.text: Person presenting Bill Porter

explanation.surface: A man named Bill Porter is introduced to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Porter reads as a name, but it splits: one who presents a bill (a cheque or note payable to bearer), and a porter, who carries loads.
explanation.definitionFit: A bearer is both the holder who presents a bill or cheque for payment and a carrier who transports loads, like a porter.

clue.text: Outlook for the soft, ware race, in new presentation

indicators.note: presenting the letters anew means the words the soft, ware and race are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something is being forecast for a software race, the clue pretending to be about computing.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma between 'soft' and 'ware' disguises the fodder, which reads together as a computing phrase; 'Outlook' also suggests the email program rather than a prediction.
explanation.definitionFit: A forecast of the weather is the meteorological outlook for the coming days.

clue.text: Cut in earnings makes one terribly frightened

indicators.note: in signals that the cut is placed inside the earnings

parts.note: pay is what one earns
a nick is a small cut

explanation.surface: Someone hearing of a pay cut becomes very frightened.
explanation.definitionFit: Panicky means overcome with sudden fear, so terribly frightened.

clue.text: Means of securing motor-cycle and sidecar

definitions.text: Means of securing motor-cycle and sidecar

parts.words: Means of securing motor-cycle and sidecar
parts.note: a motorcycle with a sidecar is called a combination in Britain, and a lock is a means of securing something, so a pun on a lock for such a vehicle

explanation.surface: Advice on how to keep a motorbike and sidecar from being stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a motorcycle with sidecar attached is known as a combination; the clue puns on the dial-operated lock.
explanation.definitionFit: A lock opened by dialling a set sequence of numbers is a security device, which is what the clue describes.

clue.text: White powder easing Ma's trouble?

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters of easing and Ma are stirred up

parts.note: Ma is taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A powder relieves Mother's indigestion.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: milk of magnesia is a classic remedy for stomach trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Magnesia is magnesium oxide, a white powder used as an antacid.

clue.text: Uncontrollable rage could give distress

indicators.note: letters that cannot be controlled run wild, so rage and give are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fits of rage cause distress.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrieve is to cause someone pain or grievance, so to distress them.

clue.text: Short-lived insects may fly close together

definitions.text: Short-lived insects may fly close together

parts.words: Short-lived insects may fly close together
parts.note: read as may fly closed up into one word, these are the mayflies, insects famously living only a day

explanation.surface: An observation that short-lived insects swarm closely in flight.
explanation.walkthrough: Close 'may fly' together and you get the mayfly, whose genus name also means things lasting only briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemera are mayflies, and more generally things that last a very short time.

clue.text: Only stove in a Dutch house

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Only stove in a Dutch house'; RANGE is the stove but no word gives the O ('Only' is not O), so a word seems lost in OCR and no source gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Only stove in a Dutch house

clue.text: Picking up the idea of the game?

definitions.text: Picking up the idea of the game?

parts.words: Picking up the idea of the game?
parts.note: an archaic verb meaning to filch or pick up is also the name of a matchstick-taking game, so the game's idea is picking things up

explanation.surface: Someone is grasping how a game works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picking up' looks like understanding, but nim is an old word for stealing, and in the game players take objects from heaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Nim is a game of removing counters from piles, and also an old word for steal.

clue.text: Books of Macbeth and Othello, for example

definitions.text: Books of Macbeth and Othello, for example

parts.words: Books of Macbeth and Othello, for example
parts.note: Macbeth and Othello are Verdi operas as well as plays, and the books of operas are their texts

explanation.surface: A remark on the published texts of two Shakespeare tragedies.
explanation.walkthrough: The plays suggest Shakespeare's scripts, but Verdi set both as operas; an opera's text is its book.
explanation.definitionFit: Libretti are the written words of operas, also called their books.

clue.text: Involving two of brainy disposition

indicators.note: a disposition is an arrangement, so the letters of brainy are set out afresh

explanation.surface: Two people share a brainy temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: Binary means composed of or relating to a pair of things.

clue.text: Recklessly, I hang about for an English author

indicators.note: about signals that the letters are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone loafs recklessly, waiting on a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recklessly' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'about' rearranges RECKLESSLY I HANG.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley was a Victorian novelist who wrote The Water-Babies and Westward Ho!.

clue.text: Port always right in Scotland

parts.note: ay is an old and Scottish word for always

explanation.surface: A Scottish harbour is said to be always correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Scotland' sits after the wordplay, placing the port and also nodding to the Scots word AY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ayr is a harbour town on the Firth of Clyde in south-west Scotland.

clue.text: Eccentric, if loud, capital

parts.note: a card is an amusing oddball
F is forte, the musical direction for loud

explanation.surface: An odd and noisy city is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an anagram signal but is a noun synonym, CARD.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales.

clue.text: Greek hero sick, with pains all round

indicators.note: the pains go all round, enclosing the word for sick

parts.note: aches are pains
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A Greek warrior lies ill and aching all over.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits: he was wounded in the heel, his one weak spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles was the champion warrior of the Greeks at Troy in the Iliad.

clue.text: In modest way, show, ing object on cathedral

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above, so the objection sits atop the cathedral

parts.note: to demur is to object
Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Someone modestly protests about a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is held as 'show, ing', an OCR break of 'showing', a link word. ELY is the crossword's favourite cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: Demurely means in a reserved, shy or decorous manner, which is modest behaviour.

clue.text: Appropriate, his function?

parts.note: appropriate read as a verb, to take for oneself, is the job of one who takes what is not his

explanation.surface: Asking whether some role is suitable for a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' looks like the adjective 'fitting', but it is the verb meaning to take illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: A stealer is one who appropriates, taking another's property.

clue.text: Be prone to equivocate

explanation.surface: Someone tends to be evasive.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie is both to rest flat on one's front or back and to tell untruths.

clue.text: A large beer called for a lady's maid

parts.note: big means large

indicators.note: called means spoken, so the word for beer is heard

parts.note: ale is a type of beer

explanation.surface: Someone orders a big beer for a lady's maid.
explanation.walkthrough: An abigail is an old term for a lady's maid, from a character in Beaumont and Fletcher's The Scornful Lady.
explanation.definitionFit: Abigail was a stock name for a waiting-woman, so it came to mean a lady's personal attendant.

clue.text: Originally, a quartet in which one player re, mained tacit

definitions.text: Originally, a quartet in which one player re, mained tacit

parts.words: Originally, a quartet in which one player re, mained tacit
parts.note: a comedy act of brothers began as four, and one of them, Harpo, never spoke

explanation.surface: A musical quartet in which one member never played a note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quartet' and 'tacit' suggest chamber music, but this is a comedy family act; held as 're, mained', an OCR break of 'remained'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marx Brothers were originally four comedians, Groucho, Chico, Harpo and Zeppo, with Harpo playing a mute.

clue.text: Puts away masses, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word for masses is spoken

parts.note: hordes are large crowds

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that someone stashes away large quantities.
explanation.definitionFit: To hoard is to stockpile, storing goods away secretly.

clue.text: Tar assessment

explanation.surface: An evaluation of tar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tar' is a sailor; in the Royal Navy a rating is a sailor without a commission.
explanation.definitionFit: A rating is a naval seaman below officer rank, and also a grading or evaluation.

clue.text: Clergyman takes chlorine little by little

parts.note: Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine
Eric, or Little by Little is a Victorian school story by F. W. Farrar

explanation.surface: A minister inhales chlorine gradually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little by little' looks like a gradual process but is the subtitle of the moralising Victorian boys' novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric is a member of the clergy, a priest or minister.

clue.text: Chivalrous chaps irritate workers

parts.note: to gall is to vex or irritate
worker ants are the classic crossword workers

explanation.surface: Gentlemanly men annoy the staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallants are dashing men attentive to women, courtly cavaliers.

clue.text: Collection of sayings in an anthology

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A book of quotations is found in an anthology.
explanation.definitionFit: Ana is a collection of a person's remarks or anecdotes, as in table talk.

clue.text: Spheres of interest in respect of charity

parts.note: re is Latin for concerning
alms are charitable gifts

explanation.surface: Fields of concern regarding giving to the poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Realms are domains or fields of activity, areas of interest.

clue.text: Disturbance in which, at home, detectives throw net out

parts.note: in means at home
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

indicators.note: throw, with out, means toss the word net about
out completes the signal that the letters of net are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Police at a house throw out a net during a disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: An incident is an occurrence, especially a violent or disruptive one.
